Source: Q&A: oldest established — Balliol College Archives (https://balliolarchivist.wordpress.com/2011/10/06/q-a-oldest-established/) Facts: Balliol founded c.1263 as a house of scholars on land owned by its founder, on its present Broad Street site, continuously since; University College traces its claim to William of Durham's 1249 bequest Source: Balliol College — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balliol_College,_Oxford) Facts: The three oldest colleges (University, Balliol, Merton) were established between 1249 and 1264; There is dispute over the exact order and when each began taking students | det_08: Rewley Abbey: the 1201 outlier that is not really a college. Source: Rewley Abbey — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rewley_Abbey) Facts: Rewley Abbey was a Cistercian monastic house with a studium near Oxford; It was dissolved during the Reformation and is not a surviving college

raw_evidence.label: Three colleges, one unsolvable argument about age
raw_evidence.content: Oxford's oldest-college title has three claimants and no referee, because each rests on a different definition of 'oldest'. University College (1249) points to the earliest money: a bequest in the 1249 will of William of Durham to support Oxford scholars. Balliol (c.1263) claims the longest unbroken physical presence — a house of scholars living on its founder's land on the present Broad Street site, continuously ever since. Merton (1264) holds the oldest formal constitution: Walter de Merton gave it statutes that made it a self-governing college, something Balliol and Univ lacked until the 1280s. All three dates fall inside a fifteen-year window, the medieval records are thin and disputed, and members of each college still cheerfully reject the others' claims. There is, in effect, no correct answer — which is exactly what makes it a good story.

raw_evidence.label: Rewley Abbey: the 1201 outlier that is not really a college
raw_evidence.content: The single oldest row in the dataset, Rewley Abbey (1201), is also the one that should not be counted as a college at all in the modern sense. It was a Cistercian monastic studium — a house where monks studied — founded on the edge of Oxford and dissolved at the Reformation. It appears because Wikidata's class definition is generous, and it sits 48 years before University College's 1249 claim. Including it would let someone say 'Oxford's oldest college dates to 1201', which is technically in the data but historically misleading. It is the clearest example of why the dataset's caveats matter: the earliest number is not the earliest college.

raw_evidence.label: The Reformation: destruction disguised as growth
raw_evidence.content: The 16th century is the single biggest century in the dataset by foundations — but much of that count is churn, not pure expansion. Henry VIII's Reformation dissolved Oxford's monastic colleges: Gloucester College fell in 1539, St Mary's College in 1540, as the suppression of the monasteries cut off the religious orders that staffed them. At the same moment, new colleges rose from the rubble, often on the same stone. Cardinal Wolsey's Cardinal College (1525) was suppressed when Wolsey fell from favour, refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532, and finally re-established by the king in 1546 as Christ Church — which doubles as the cathedral of the new Diocese of Oxford. So the 16th-century 'boom' is partly a single institution being killed and reborn under three names, all of which survive as separate rows in the data.

raw_evidence.label: 1878–1893: the women's colleges arrive
raw_evidence.content: The 19th-century cluster in the data is not just more colleges — it is a change in who Oxford was for. Lady Margaret Hall (1878) was the first women's college; Somerville opened in 1879, splitting from LMH over religious denomination. St Anne's (1879), St Hugh's (1886) and St Hilda's (1893) followed within fifteen years. The catch: these colleges existed for decades before women could actually take Oxford degrees. Women attended lectures and sat examinations but were not full members of the University until 1920. So a row dated 1878 marks the founding of an institution whose students could not graduate for another forty-two years — the dataset records the building before it records the right.

Reuben is the newest college in the dataset and the first new college at Oxford since Kellogg in 1990. It was approved by Congregation in May 2019 as 'Parks College', then renamed after an £80 million gift from the Reuben Foundation in 2020, and took its first graduate students in 2021 in the former Radcliffe Science Library. Green Templeton (2008) is a different kind of entry: it is a merger of Green College and Templeton College (1965), which is why both Templeton and Green Templeton appear as separate rows — the data captures a marriage and both of its partners.

raw_evidence.label: The Reformation: destruction disguised as growth
raw_evidence.content: The 16th century is the single biggest century in the dataset by foundations — but much of that count is churn, not pure expansion. Henry VIII's Reformation dissolved Oxford's monastic colleges: Gloucester College fell in 1539, St Mary's College in 1540, as the suppression of the monasteries cut off the religious orders that staffed them. At the same moment, new colleges rose from the rubble, often on the same stone. Cardinal Wolsey's Cardinal College (1525) was suppressed when Wolsey fell from favour, refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532, and finally re-established by the king in 1546 as Christ Church — which doubles as the cathedral of the new Diocese of Oxford. So the 16th-century 'boom' is partly a single institution being killed and reborn under three names, all of which survive as separate rows in the data.

raw_evidence.label: 1878–1893: the women's colleges arrive
raw_evidence.content: The 19th-century cluster in the data is not just more colleges — it is a change in who Oxford was for. Lady Margaret Hall (1878) was the first women's college; Somerville opened in 1879, splitting from LMH over religious denomination. St Anne's (1879), St Hugh's (1886) and St Hilda's (1893) followed within fifteen years. The catch: these colleges existed for decades before women could actually take Oxford degrees. Women attended lectures and sat examinations but were not full members of the University until 1920. So a row dated 1878 marks the founding of an institution whose students could not graduate for another forty-two years — the dataset records the building before it records the right.

raw_evidence.label: The modern wave: philanthropists, mergers, and Reuben (2019)
raw_evidence.content: The 20th–21st century foundations are dominated by graduate colleges endowed by industrial and financial wealth: Nuffield (1937, the motor magnate Lord Nuffield), Wolfson (1965, Isaac Wolfson), Kellogg (1990, the cereal fortune) and Reuben (2019). Reuben is the newest college in the dataset and the first new college at Oxford since Kellogg in 1990. It was approved by Congregation in May 2019 as 'Parks College', then renamed after an £80 million gift from the Reuben Foundation in 2020, and took its first graduate students in 2021 in the former Radcliffe Science Library. Green Templeton (2008) is a different kind of entry: it is a merger of Green College and Templeton College (1965), which is why both Templeton and Green Templeton appear as separate rows — the data captures a marriage and both of its partners.

raw_evidence.label: Half-century view: the Victorian spike
raw_evidence.content: Bucketing foundations into 50-year windows sharpens the modern wave to a single point. The 1850–1899 window holds 9 colleges — more than any other half-century in 800 years — driven by Keble (1870), Hertford's refounding (1874) and the burst of women's colleges (1878–1893). The 1950–1999 window holds 7, a second modern surge of graduate colleges. Nothing in the medieval or early-modern record comes close to the Victorian rate; the densest medieval window (1250–1299) holds 5. The data's busiest fifty years are the most recent ones a Victorian would have lived through, not the founding centuries.

raw_evidence.label: The two waves
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: 9 colleges each in 19th and 20th c.; 1850-1899 window = 9. Keep barbell framing.

raw_evidence.label: The Reformation: destruction disguised as growth
raw_evidence.content: The 16th century is the single biggest century in the dataset by foundations — but much of that count is churn, not pure expansion. Henry VIII's Reformation dissolved Oxford's monastic colleges: Gloucester College fell in 1539, St Mary's College in 1540, as the suppression of the monasteries cut off the religious orders that staffed them. At the same moment, new colleges rose from the rubble, often on the same stone. Cardinal Wolsey's Cardinal College (1525) was suppressed when Wolsey fell from favour, refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532, and finally re-established by the king in 1546 as Christ Church — which doubles as the cathedral of the new Diocese of Oxford. So the 16th-century 'boom' is partly a single institution being killed and reborn under three names, all of which survive as separate rows in the data.

raw_evidence.label: 1878–1893: the women's colleges arrive
raw_evidence.content: The 19th-century cluster in the data is not just more colleges — it is a change in who Oxford was for. Lady Margaret Hall (1878) was the first women's college; Somerville opened in 1879, splitting from LMH over religious denomination. St Anne's (1879), St Hugh's (1886) and St Hilda's (1893) followed within fifteen years. The catch: these colleges existed for decades before women could actually take Oxford degrees. Women attended lectures and sat examinations but were not full members of the University until 1920. So a row dated 1878 marks the founding of an institution whose students could not graduate for another forty-two years — the dataset records the building before it records the right.

raw_evidence.label: A 156-year silence, and an 18th century with one college
raw_evidence.content: The single most striking gap in the founding record runs from Worcester College's predecessor in 1714 to Keble in 1870 — a 156-year stretch with almost no new colleges. The 18th century produces exactly one foundation in the dataset (Worcester, 1714). Other long gaps appear (75 years from 1624 to 1699, then 51, 48, 48 years earlier on), but nothing matches the Georgian silence. After the medieval rush and the Tudor Reformation churn, Oxford essentially stopped founding colleges for a century and a half — then opened the floodgates in the Victorian era. The quiet middle of the barbell is not gradual; it is a near-total halt.

sentences.summary: det_03: The Reformation: destruction disguised as growth. Source: Christ Church, Oxford — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church,_Oxford) Facts: Cardinal College was suppressed after Wolsey's fall and refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532; Refounded as Christ Church in 1546, also serving as the cathedral of the Diocese of Oxford Source: Timeline of Oxford — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Oxford) Facts: Gloucester College dissolved 1539; St Mary's College dissolved 1540

raw_evidence.label: The Reformation: destruction disguised as growth
raw_evidence.content: The 16th century is the single biggest century in the dataset by foundations — but much of that count is churn, not pure expansion. Henry VIII's Reformation dissolved Oxford's monastic colleges: Gloucester College fell in 1539, St Mary's College in 1540, as the suppression of the monasteries cut off the religious orders that staffed them. At the same moment, new colleges rose from the rubble, often on the same stone. Cardinal Wolsey's Cardinal College (1525) was suppressed when Wolsey fell from favour, refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532, and finally re-established by the king in 1546 as Christ Church — which doubles as the cathedral of the new Diocese of Oxford. So the 16th-century 'boom' is partly a single institution being killed and reborn under three names, all of which survive as separate rows in the data.

raw_evidence.label: Roughly 1 in 5 rows is not a living college
raw_evidence.content: The dataset deliberately mixes survivors with the dead. Eleven of the 50 rows are defunct, dissolved, merged, or not residential colleges at all: Rewley Abbey, Gloucester, Durham, Canterbury, Cardinal, King Henry VIII's, St Mary's, St Bernard's and Greek College (all dissolved or vanished), Templeton (merged into Green Templeton in 2008), and Examination Schools (an administrative building, not a college). Removing these leaves roughly 39 surviving colleges — the figure usually quoted for Oxford today. Any statistic about 'the typical Oxford college' that uses all 50 rows is silently averaging in eight-century-old ghosts.

raw_evidence.label: 1878–1893: the women's colleges arrive
raw_evidence.content: The 19th-century cluster in the data is not just more colleges — it is a change in who Oxford was for. Lady Margaret Hall (1878) was the first women's college; Somerville opened in 1879, splitting from LMH over religious denomination. St Anne's (1879), St Hugh's (1886) and St Hilda's (1893) followed within fifteen years. The catch: these colleges existed for decades before women could actually take Oxford degrees. Women attended lectures and sat examinations but were not full members of the University until 1920. So a row dated 1878 marks the founding of an institution whose students could not graduate for another forty-two years — the dataset records the building before it records the right.

raw_evidence.label: Half-century view: the Victorian spike
raw_evidence.content: Bucketing foundations into 50-year windows sharpens the modern wave to a single point. The 1850–1899 window holds 9 colleges — more than any other half-century in 800 years — driven by Keble (1870), Hertford's refounding (1874) and the burst of women's colleges (1878–1893). The 1950–1999 window holds 7, a second modern surge of graduate colleges. Nothing in the medieval or early-modern record comes close to the Victorian rate; the densest medieval window (1250–1299) holds 5. The data's busiest fifty years are the most recent ones a Victorian would have lived through, not the founding centuries.

raw_evidence.label: Half-century view: the Victorian spike
raw_evidence.content: Bucketing foundations into 50-year windows sharpens the modern wave to a single point. The 1850–1899 window holds 9 colleges — more than any other half-century in 800 years — driven by Keble (1870), Hertford's refounding (1874) and the burst of women's colleges (1878–1893). The 1950–1999 window holds 7, a second modern surge of graduate colleges. Nothing in the medieval or early-modern record comes close to the Victorian rate; the densest medieval window (1250–1299) holds 5. The data's busiest fifty years are the most recent ones a Victorian would have lived through, not the founding centuries.

raw_evidence.label: Founders: 27 people, only three founded twice
raw_evidence.content: Of 50 colleges, 28 record a founder; after splitting the semicolon-separated joint foundations, there are 27 distinct founders. Almost everyone founded exactly one college. Only three names appear twice: Thomas Wolsey (Cardinal College and, jointly, Christ Church), Henry VIII (King Henry VIII's College and Christ Church), and Elizabeth Wordsworth, who founded both Lady Margaret Hall (1878) and St Hugh's (1886) for women. The Wolsey and Henry repeats are really the same Reformation institution under successive names; Wordsworth's are two genuinely separate women's colleges, making her arguably the most productive single founder in the dataset.

sentences.summary: det_06: Coats of arms and namesakes as a social history. Source: Colleges of the University of Oxford — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleges_of_the_University_of_Oxford) Facts: Colleges were founded by a mix of clergy, royalty and modern philanthropists; College coats of arms frequently derive from the arms of the founder or namesake

raw_evidence.label: Coats of arms and namesakes as a social history
raw_evidence.content: Read the founder and namesake columns top to bottom and you get a compact social history of who held wealth and power in England across eight centuries. The medieval founders are bishops and royal clerks — Walter de Merton, William of Wykeham, William Waynflete. The Tudor era brings monarchs and prelates — Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, Cardinal Wolsey, Bishop Foxe. The modern era brings industrialists and financiers — Lord Nuffield, Isaac Wolfson, the Reuben brothers. The namesakes split the same way: early colleges are named for saints and feast days (Mary Magdalene, John the Baptist, All Souls' Day, the Holy Trinity), while later ones are named for the benefactor's own surname. The colleges' heraldic coats of arms encode this lineage visually — each crest borrows the arms of its founder or patron — which is why the real crests are the natural visual spine for this story.

raw_evidence.content: 37 of 50 colleges record a namesake, and they split almost evenly: 17 are religious (saints, feast days, holy figures — Mary Magdalene, John the Baptist, All Souls' Day, the Holy Trinity, Jesus Christ) and 20 are personal or secular (founders, royal consorts, scholars, philanthropists — Walter de Merton, Philippa of Hainault, Mary Somerville, Isaac Wolfson). The split is not random across time: religious namesakes dominate the medieval and Tudor colleges, while the 19th- and 20th-century foundations are overwhelmingly named after a person — often the benefactor whose money built them. The namesake column is, in effect, a record of England's slow secularisation of patronage.

raw_evidence.label: Coats of arms and namesakes as a social history
raw_evidence.content: Read the founder and namesake columns top to bottom and you get a compact social history of who held wealth and power in England across eight centuries. The medieval founders are bishops and royal clerks — Walter de Merton, William of Wykeham, William Waynflete. The Tudor era brings monarchs and prelates — Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, Cardinal Wolsey, Bishop Foxe. The modern era brings industrialists and financiers — Lord Nuffield, Isaac Wolfson, the Reuben brothers. The namesakes split the same way: early colleges are named for saints and feast days (Mary Magdalene, John the Baptist, All Souls' Day, the Holy Trinity), while later ones are named for the benefactor's own surname. The colleges' heraldic coats of arms encode this lineage visually — each crest borrows the arms of its founder or patron — which is why the real crests are the natural visual spine for this story.

raw_evidence.label: Dataset shape and where the gaps are
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is 50 rows by 7 columns, one row per college, with founding years spanning 1201 to 2019 — 818 years. Coverage is wildly uneven across columns. The motto field is essentially empty: 49 of 50 colleges record no motto, with only Magdalen's 'Floreat Magdalena!' surviving. Founder is blank for 22 colleges, namesake for 13, website for 10, and two colleges (Harris Manchester and St Bernard's) have no founding year at all and must be excluded from any date-based analysis. The sparsity is informative rather than sloppy: Wikidata records who founded and named a college far more reliably than its Latin motto, and the missing founders cluster among the oldest, murkiest monastic houses.

# --- ana_02: Foundations per century (two waves) ---
print("\n=== ana_02 ===")
cent_rows = list(csv.DictReader(open(CENT, encoding="utf-8")))
for cr in cent_rows:
    print(f"  {cr['century']}: {cr['colleges_founded']}")
known = [(cr['century'], int(cr['colleges_founded'])) for cr in cent_rows if cr['century'] != 'unknown']
peak = max(known, key=lambda x: x[1])
print(f"peak century: {peak[0]} with {peak[1]}")
print(f"13th+14th medieval = {7+5}; 19th+20th modern = {9+9}")
# end ana_02

# --- ana_03: The oldest-college cluster (15-year window) ---
print("\n=== ana_03 ===")
ordered = sorted(have_year, key=year)

It was approved by Congregation in May 2019 as 'Parks College', then renamed after an £80 million gift from the Reuben Foundation in 2020, and took its first graduate students in 2021 in the former Radcliffe Science Library. Green Templeton (2008) is a different kind of entry: it is a merger of Green College and Templeton College (1965), which is why both Templeton and Green Templeton appear as separate rows — the data captures a marriage and both of its partners.

raw_evidence.label: Caveats the analyst must respect
raw_evidence.content: Several traps lurk in the data. (1) It blends current colleges with defunct, dissolved and merged ones — Rewley Abbey, Gloucester, Durham, Canterbury, Cardinal, King Henry VIII's, St Mary's, St Bernard's, Greek College, Templeton, Examination Schools — so any 'typical Oxford college' statistic must separate the ~39 survivors from the full historical set. (2) Two rows (Harris Manchester, St Bernard's) have a blank founding year and must be dropped from year-based math. (3) Medieval dates are approximate and disputed; 1249/1263/1264 are nominal. (4) Founder and namesake fields are often blank and sometimes hold multiple semicolon-separated names (Balliol, Christ Church, Green Templeton) that must be split before counting people. (5) The century table includes an 'unknown' bucket of 2 — the two blank-year colleges.
